Pantoliano has met with both the Obama and McCain camps to advocate for mental health and recovery. As founder and president of the eight-month-old advocacy organization No Kidding, Me Too, he unveiled a teaser of his new film exploring various forms of mental illness. At the CNN Grill, he answered five questions for CNN.com.

**CNN.com: What brings you out here to Denver?**

Pantoliano: I've been fascinated by the political process ever since I was a child. ... I've always loved the festive spirit, the camaraderie, the dedication to a candidate—whether it was someone in the 3rd Ward of Hoboken, New Jersey, where I grew up, or a senator, a congressman, or even a visiting president. I remember when President Kennedy came to Hoboken in '61, when I was just 10 years old. And tonight, I was with the Kennedys.

**CNN.com: Are you a Barack Obama supporter?**

Pantoliano: I'm here advocating for my organization. I'll be attending the Republican National Convention next week as well. I'm speaking about mental illness and the miracles of recovery—that's what the film is about. I've met with Obama's chief of staff and his team, and I've met with McCain's people. Mental illness is at the forefront of their minds.

**CNN.com: Who are you voting for?**

Pantoliano: I don't know yet.

Watch how celebrity endorsements can backfire »

**CNN.com: Where are the hot spots in Denver? Where is everyone gathering?**

Pantoliano: Right here, at the CNN Grill. It's all anyone's talking about. I really like Denver. The security feels less intense than it was four years ago. That pervasive sense of fear this administration has instilled in us—I think I have post-traumatic stress from it. What happened was, I became addicted to the news.

iReport.com: Are you in Denver? Share sights and sounds.

**CNN.com: Do you think attending a convention helps you make up your mind better than sitting in your living room?**

Pantoliano: I'm an independent. I can be inspired tonight by Michelle Obama's speech, and then something might happen next week—so I'm constantly going back and forth. I'm a flip-flopper. The difference I see between the Republicans and the Democrats is that the Democrats truly embody the melting pot of our society. Obama genuinely represents that. Obama represents what America is today.

# Actor Joe Pantoliano Brings Mental Health Advocacy to Democratic Convention

**CNN.com** — Actor Joe Pantoliano, known for his roles in "The Sopranos," "The Matrix" and "Memento," made an appearance at the 2008 Democratic National Convention in Denver, not to talk about Hollywood, but to raise awareness about mental illness through his advocacy organization, No Kidding, Me Too!

The Emmy-winning actor, who has spoken openly about his own struggles with clinical depression, sat down with CNN to discuss his mission to combat the stigma surrounding mental health issues.

**CNN: What brought you to the Democratic National Convention this week?**

Pantoliano: I'm here because mental illness is one of the most under-discussed public health issues in this country, and political conventions are where the national conversation happens. I founded No Kidding, Me Too! to eliminate the stigma attached to brain disease. If we can get lawmakers and voters thinking about this, we can start changing policy and changing minds.

**CNN: Tell us about your organization. What does "No Kidding, Me Too!" mean?**

Pantoliano: The name comes from the reaction people have when someone finally admits they're struggling. You say, "I have depression," and suddenly the other person says, "No kidding, me too!" There's this incredible relief in discovering you're not alone. Our goal is to empower people with mental illness to feel a sense of dignity and hope, and to encourage them to seek help without shame.

**CNN: You've been candid about your own diagnosis. How did that shape this work?**

Pantoliano: For years I self-medicated and didn't understand what was wrong with me. When I was finally diagnosed with clinical depression, it was a turning point. I realized how many people suffer in silence because they're afraid of being labeled. I have a good life, a successful career, a loving family — and I still got sick. That's the point. This is a disease, like diabetes or heart disease. It's not a character flaw.

**CNN: Why do you think stigma remains such a barrier?**

Pantoliano: Because we treat the brain differently than any other organ in the body. If your pancreas is sick, nobody judges you. But if your brain is sick, people think you're weak or dangerous or unstable. That fear keeps people from getting treatment. Millions go undiagnosed and untreated every year, and some of them don't survive. Changing that language and that perception is everything.

**CNN: What do you hope people take away from your message here?**

Pantoliano: I want people to understand that recovery is possible and that asking for help is an act of courage, not weakness. If sharing my story helps one person pick up the phone and call a doctor, then this is all worth it. We're all in this together — no kidding.

For more information about mental health resources, viewers can contact the National Alliance on Mental Illness or their local health provider.

*Editor's note: If you or someone you know is struggling, help is available. In the United States, you can reach mental health support services through national and local organizations.*

# Sopranos Star Brings Mental Health Message to Denver Convention

*An interview exploring the intersection of celebrity advocacy and mental health awareness*

---

**INTERVIEWER:** Thanks for sitting down with us. You're here in Denver for the Democratic National Convention, but not necessarily for the political theater. Can you tell us what brought you here?

**ACTOR:** Absolutely, and thank you for having me. Look, I've been fortunate to have this platform because of the show, and I decided a while back that I wanted to use it for something that actually matters to me. Mental health awareness—that's the reason I'm here. A convention like this brings together thousands of people, media from all over, decision-makers. It's an opportunity to get a conversation going.

**INTERVIEWER:** Was there a personal connection that drew you to this cause?

**ACTOR:** There always is, isn't there? I don't want to get too deep into private family matters, but I'll say I've seen firsthand what it looks like when someone you love is struggling and doesn't have anywhere to turn. The stigma is real. People suffer in silence because they think there's something shameful about it. That's what I want to help change.

**INTERVIEWER:** Interestingly, your character on the show dealt with therapy quite prominently. Did that shape how you think about these issues?

**ACTOR:** *(laughs)* You know, that's the irony that a lot of people point out. The show actually did something kind of radical for its time—it put a tough, intimidating guy in a therapist's office and treated it seriously. Millions of people watched a character wrestle with anxiety, with depression, with panic attacks. I think that opened some doors in living rooms across the country. If a character like that could sit on a couch and talk about his feelings, maybe the guy watching at home could too.

**INTERVIEWER:** Do you think entertainment has a responsibility in this space?

**ACTOR:** I think entertainment has *influence*, and with influence comes some responsibility, yeah. I'm not saying every show needs to be a public service announcement—God, that would be boring. But when you have a chance to portray these things honestly, without turning them into a punchline or a plot device, you should take it seriously. Real people are watching who see themselves reflected up there.

**INTERVIEWER:** What are you hoping to accomplish specifically here at the DNC?

**ACTOR:** I'm meeting with a few advocacy organizations, talking to some folks about funding for community mental health programs. That's really the nuts and bolts of it. The awareness stuff is great, but awareness without resources is just noise. People need access to care—affordable, accessible, without a six-month waiting list. That's what I'm pushing for in these conversations.

**INTERVIEWER:** Do you worry about being seen as just another celebrity attaching their name to a cause?

**ACTOR:** *(nods)* Sure, that's a fair concern, and I think about it. Nobody wants to be the guy who shows up for a photo op and then disappears. That's why I try to actually show up—do the reading, meet the professionals, listen to people who've lived it. I'm an actor, I'm not a clinician or a policy expert. My job here is to help amplify voices that are usually a lot quieter than mine. If I can point the spotlight somewhere useful, that's a good day's work.

**INTERVIEWER:** Any final message for people watching at home who might be struggling?

**ACTOR:** Yeah. Just—you're not alone, and there's no shame in it. Reaching out for help isn't weakness. Some of the toughest people I've ever known have been in therapy. Talk to somebody. A friend, a doctor, a hotline, whoever. The worst thing you can do is carry it by yourself. That's the whole reason I'm standing here.

**INTERVIEWER:** Thank you so much for your time.

**ACTOR:** My pleasure. Thanks for helping get the word out.

---

*If you or someone you know is struggling, help is available. In the U.S., you can call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.*

# CNN Convention Coverage: Mental Health Advocacy Takes Center Stage

**Interview conducted on the convention floor**

---

**CNN CORRESPONDENT:** Thanks for joining us amid all the excitement here. A lot of celebrities come to these conventions to endorse candidates, but you've made it clear that's not why you're here. Tell us what brought you.

**CELEBRITY:** Absolutely, and thanks for having me. You're right—I'm not here to tell anyone who to vote for. I'm here because mental health is on the ballot in a bigger sense. Regardless of party, this is an issue that touches every family in this country, and I want that conversation happening in rooms like this one.

**CNN CORRESPONDENT:** Why keep it nonpartisan? Some would argue that endorsing candidates is how you actually move policy.

**CELEBRITY:** I understand that view, but here's my thinking: the moment I slap a partisan label on mental health, I lose half the audience I'm trying to reach. Depression doesn't check your voter registration. Anxiety doesn't care who you supported last election. I want a mom in a red state and a college kid in a blue city to both feel like this message is for them.

**CNN CORRESPONDENT:** You've been open about your own struggles. How much does that personal history drive this?

**CELEBRITY:** Completely. There was a period in my life where I had every external marker of success and I was privately falling apart. I didn't have the language for what I was going through, and I certainly didn't feel like I could say it out loud. If I can help even a few people skip that isolation I felt, that's worth more to me than any red carpet.

**CNN CORRESPONDENT:** What specifically are you asking policymakers—of any party—to do?

**CELEBRITY:** Three things, mainly. First, real funding for the crisis response system, including the 988 hotline, so that when someone reaches out, someone actually reaches back. Second, mental health parity—insurance should cover a therapy appointment the same way it covers a broken arm. And third, we need to meet young people where they are, which means resources in schools and honest conversations about social media.

**CNN CORRESPONDENT:** Social media—that's a tough one, especially given your own presence on those platforms.

**CELEBRITY:** *(laughs)* It's a real tension, and I won't pretend otherwise. These tools connect us, but they can also be engineered to keep us comparing and scrolling at two in the morning. I'm not anti-technology. I'm pro being intentional about it. I'd love to see more transparency about how these platforms affect developing brains.

**CNN CORRESPONDENT:** You'll be walking past a lot of candidates this week who'd love a photo with you. What do you say to them?

**CELEBRITY:** The same thing I'd say to candidates at the other convention: show me your plan. Don't give me a sound bite in an election year and then forget the issue in November. Fund the programs. Support the caregivers, the nurses, the counselors doing this work for very little recognition. I'll cheer for anyone from either party who actually delivers.

**CNN CORRESPONDENT:** For someone watching right now who's struggling, what do you want them to hear?

**CELEBRITY:** That you're not weak, and you're not alone, and reaching out is the strongest thing you can do. If you're in crisis, please call or text 988. Talk to someone. The version of you on the other side of this—they're worth fighting for. I promise you that.

**CNN CORRESPONDENT:** Powerful note to end on. Thank you for being here.

**CELEBRITY:** Thank you for giving this the airtime. That matters more than you know.

---

*The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is available 24/7 by calling or texting 988.*

# Star Power Meets Politics: A Q&A at the Convention Floor

*By Staff Writer | 2008*

The convention hall buzzed with energy as delegates filed past, but a crowd had gathered around a familiar face—an accomplished actor who has increasingly traded scripts for stump speeches in recent years. Known for his blockbuster roles and, more recently, his outspoken advocacy work, he agreed to sit down with us amid the political spectacle.

Wearing a crisp blazer and a delegate credential around his neck, he spoke candidly about his political awakening, his upcoming film, and—perhaps surprisingly—why he still hasn't made up his mind about November.

---

**Q: You've become a fixture at political events lately. What drew you here?**

"I think there's a moment happening in this country right now, and I wanted to witness it firsthand. It's easy to shout opinions from Hollywood, but I wanted to actually be in the room, listen to the delegates, hear the debates. This is democracy in its rawest form—messy, loud, imperfect. I love it."

**Q: A lot of celebrities pick a side early. You've held back. Why?**

"Honestly? Because I don't think either party has fully earned my vote yet. I know that's not a popular thing to say. People want you to wear a jersey and root for a team. But I've got real questions about the economy, about how we get out of these wars, about health care. I'm listening to both conventions. I owe it to myself—and to the folks who follow what I say—to actually think it through."

**Q: Does being undecided invite criticism?**

"Oh, sure. I get it from both directions. One side calls me a fence-sitter, the other assumes I'm secretly against them. But I'd rather be honestly undecided than dishonestly committed. I've been reading the position papers, I've talked to advisors from both campaigns. I want substance, not slogans."

**Q: Let's talk about the new film. What can you tell us?**

"It's the project I'm most proud of, and it actually ties into why I'm here. It's a story about ordinary people caught up in forces bigger than themselves—political forces, economic ones. Without giving too much away, it asks what we owe each other as citizens. We shot it over eight months, and it changed how I see a lot of these issues."

**Q: Did making the film influence your political views?**

"Absolutely. You can't spend that much time inhabiting a character who's struggling—losing a job, worrying about his kids' future—without it getting under your skin. Art has a way of making the abstract personal. I walked away from that set thinking harder about policy than I ever had before."

**Q: What issues will ultimately decide your vote?**

"The economy is front and center for everybody right now—you'd have to be blind not to see the storm clouds. But for me, it's also about leadership and temperament. Who's going to unite people instead of dividing them? Who has a real plan versus who just has good speechwriters? I'll know it when I hear it. I'm still waiting."

**Q: Any advice for other undecided voters watching this convention?**

"Don't let anyone rush you. Do your homework. Watch both sides make their case. This is one of the most important decisions we make, and it's okay to take it seriously enough to still be thinking. Being undecided isn't apathy—for me, it's the opposite. It means I still care enough to be persuaded."

---

As the interview wrapped, a delegate called out for a photo, and he obliged with an easy grin. Whether his eventual endorsement swings a single vote remains to be seen—but in a season defined by fervent certainty on all sides, his willingness to remain openly undecided struck a notably different chord.

His film opens in theaters this fall.

---

*Would you like me to tailor this piece toward a specific convention (Democratic or Republican), name a fictional actor and film, or adjust the tone to be more satirical or more serious?*

# "No Kidding, Me Too": A Conversation with Joe Pantoliano

*The veteran actor, known for roles in "The Matrix," "The Sopranos," and "Memento," has spent years fighting to destigmatize mental illness. In this conversation, he discusses his advocacy organization and his political engagement.*

---

**Q: For readers unfamiliar with your advocacy work, what is "No Kidding, Me Too" and what inspired you to found it?**

A: "No Kidding, Me Too" grew out of my own journey with depression. After I was diagnosed, I realized how much shame surrounded mental illness—including my own shame. The name captures the whole idea: when someone admits they're struggling, someone else can say, "No kidding, me too." That moment of recognition breaks the isolation. The organization aims to remove the stigma attached to brain disease so people can seek treatment without embarrassment.

**Q: You use the term "brain disease" rather than "mental illness." Why is that distinction important to you?**

A: Language matters enormously. When we say "mental illness," people hear something about character or willpower—like you should just snap out of it. But these are physical conditions of an organ, the brain, just like heart disease affects the heart. Reframing it as a disease of an organ helps people understand it's medical, not a moral failing. That shift in language can be the difference between someone getting help or suffering in silence.

**Q: How did your own diagnosis change your perspective on the work you needed to do?**

A: I spent decades self-medicating and not understanding what was wrong with me. I was successful by any external measure, but I was miserable inside and didn't know why. Getting diagnosed was liberating, but it also made me angry—angry that we don't talk about this, angry at how many people suffer needlessly. I decided I had a platform and I should use it. If Joey Pants can stand up and say he has depression, maybe that gives permission to somebody else.

**Q: Let's talk about your political engagement. What drew you to bring your advocacy to the Democratic National Convention?**

A: A convention is where the national conversation happens, where policy priorities get set. I wanted mental health to be part of that conversation. Too often it's an afterthought—we talk about it only after a tragedy. I went to remind people that this affects millions of families, including veterans coming home, kids in schools, working people. It's not a partisan issue, but you have to show up where decisions get made.

**Q: What were your experiences like there? Did you find people receptive to your message?**

A: Overwhelmingly, yes. What struck me most was how many people pulled me aside privately to share their own stories—a delegate whose son struggled, a staffer dealing with anxiety, people who'd lost family members to suicide. That's the "me too" phenomenon in action. Behind the scenes, everyone is touched by this. The challenge is moving it from whispered conversations to public policy and open dialogue.

**Q: Did you encounter any resistance or frustration in that environment?**

A: The frustration is always the same: politicians will nod and agree it's important, but funding and legislation lag behind the sentiment. Mental health parity—making insurance cover brain disease the way it covers other illnesses—has been a long fight. I push people to move past sympathy toward action. Nice words don't get anyone treatment.

**Q: How do you respond to skeptics who might see a celebrity advocate as just lending a famous face to a cause?**

A: I understand the skepticism, and I welcome it. But this isn't a photo op for me—it's my life. I've lived the depression, the shame, the recovery. The fame is just a tool. If my name gets people to listen for thirty seconds longer, then I've done my job. I'd rather be known for this work than for any movie I've made.

**Q: What role does storytelling play in your approach, given your background as an actor?**

A: Storytelling is everything. Statistics don't move people—stories do. That's why we've done documentary work, because when you see a real person's face and hear their words, you can't dismiss them as a category. I'm a storyteller by trade, so I use that skill. I want people to feel less alone, and the way you do that is by telling the truth about your own experience.

**Q: What's your ultimate goal—what does success look like for "No Kidding, Me Too"?**

A: Success is a world where someone can say "I have depression" as easily as "I have diabetes," and get the same compassion and care. It's a world where kids learn about brain health in school, where veterans get treatment without judgment, where insurance covers it fully. I may not see all of it in my lifetime, but if we move the needle on the stigma, that's a legacy worth fighting for.

**Q: Any final thoughts for readers who might be struggling themselves?**

A: You're not alone, and there's no shame in it. Reach out—to a doctor, a friend, a hotline, anyone. The bravest thing you can do is ask for help. And when you find the courage to say what you're going through, I promise someone will look at you and say, "No kidding—me too."

---

*Joe Pantoliano continues his advocacy work through public speaking, documentary filmmaking, and outreach efforts aimed at changing how society understands and discusses brain disease.*
